1 · Price growth and the last peak

Change in the 12-month median sale price over the last 1 to 5 years, to . Last peak is the most recent high that was followed by a fall of 5% or more. Below it, stagnant is how long prices took to get back above that peak, or how long they've been below it so far if they haven't recovered yet. Click a column heading to sort. Click a region to open its price history.

Darker = more growth (shaded within each column)Buying region ▲

Growth uses Cotality's 12-month median sale price for each council area (capitals: Greater Capital City area). Markets with fewer than 100 sales a year are left out. "No 5% fall since 2000" means the 12-month median never fell 5% from a high in that time. Small markets can show jumps from a handful of sales. In the charts, the short break in mid-2018 is where Cotality changed its data series; capital cities can show a small step there.

2 · Rent growth vs price growth

The gap is rent growth minus price growth over the same period, in percentage points. A positive gap means rents rose faster than prices, so rental yields widened and the market got cheaper relative to its rent. That's the "prices stagnant while rents keep rising" pattern. A negative gap means prices outran rents. Each cell shows the gap, with the rent and price changes behind it underneath. Columns are the period: 1 year to 5 years. Click a region to chart its rent and price history.

Rents rose faster than pricesPrices rose faster than rents

Rent = Cotality median asking rent (12 months); price = 12-month median sale price. Both are for the same property type and council area. Yield now = Cotality median gross rental yield.

3 · Days on market and stock on market

Days on market is the median number of days a property takes to sell over the last 12 months. Traffic Lights bands: ≤16 green (selling fast: the crowd is in), 17–44 orange, ≥45 red (slow). Stock on market is the share of all dwellings listed for sale over the last 12 months. Listings is the number of properties listed over the last 12 months. Falling days on market, stock and listings mean supply is drying up. Click a region to chart its history.

Selling faster / fewer listings than beforeSelling slower / more listings

Source: Cotality Market Trends (12-month figures). Cotality changed how it measures listings, stock on market and days on market in July 2018, so earlier figures aren't comparable and the charts start in August 2018.

4 · Vacancy rate

Vacancy rate is the share of rental properties sitting empty, as a 3-month average to . Bands: below 2% tight (the Trading Strategy entry condition), 2–3% balanced, 3%+ loose. The 12-month average smooths out monthly noise, and is shown against the 12 months before. Low or falling vacancy usually comes before rent rises (see section 2 for rent vs price). Click a region to chart its vacancy history.

Vacancy fallingVacancy rising

Vacancy: Cotality, monthly, by council area and Greater Capital City area, to Jun 2026. Each figure is a 3-month average; the 10-year average covers Jul 2016 – Jun 2026. Early years in small markets can be noisy.

5 · Building approvals and new households

New dwellings approved each financial year (July–June). Approvals turn into finished homes about 1–2 years later, so they show the supply coming. Each region is compared with its own 10-year average (FY17–26) and 15-year average (FY12–26). Use the Houses / Units toggle to switch between house approvals and unit & townhouse approvals. Showing approvals. When we entered, our buying regions' approvals vs their previous 10-year average were: . The last columns compare all approvals with new households (population added ÷ average household size): above 1.0 households per approval means supply isn't keeping up. FY26 households are estimated at the 5-year average pace because FY26 population isn't out yet. Click a region to chart its 15-year history.

Unit type
Below its long-term average (supply limited)Above its long-term average (more supply coming)

Source: ABS Building Approvals (data.api.abs.gov.au), new dwellings. FY2019–26 by council area; capital cities use the Greater Capital City area. FY2012–18 for regional areas is estimated from the nearest SA3 statistical areas, scaled to the council area. That estimate is less reliable for Bunbury, Rockhampton, Launceston and Wodonga (marked *). "Units & townhouses" = all dwellings other than detached houses (ABS "other residential"), split into apartments (flats and units in blocks) and townhouses & villas (semi-detached, row and terrace houses, townhouses and attached villa units). Cotality's "units" prices include both. Where a region averages fewer than 30 a year, it's marked low volume and not shaded, because a few approvals swing the percentage a lot. Per 1,000 residents uses each region's latest population. Household size: the sourced 2026 figure used by PP's VR Projection tool (ABS 3236.0 for capitals, state LGA projections for regional areas, PP's 2.4 assumption for Bunbury, Mandurah and Launceston), held constant. Not every approval gets built and some replace demolished homes, so treat households per approval as a direction-of-travel signal. Very small counts (e.g. Launceston's 0 units and townhouses in FY26) are as reported by the ABS and can swing a lot in percentage terms.

6 · Population change

Estimated resident population at 30 June each year (ABS). Growth by year shows how fast each region added people, against its 5 and 10-year averages. Where FY25's growth came from splits the increase into natural (births minus deaths), internal migration (people moving in from elsewhere in Australia, minus those leaving) and overseas migration. Positive internal migration means Australians are choosing to move there, which tends to drive housing demand most directly. Population is the same for houses and units. Click a region to chart its history.

Darker = faster growthMore people moving in from elsewhere in AustraliaMore moving out

Source: ABS Regional population (3218.0): estimated resident population by council area 2001–2025, and components of change FY22–FY25. Capital cities are the sum of their council areas (e.g. 30 for Melbourne), so they differ slightly from the official Greater Capital City totals. Canberra's components are for the whole ACT.

7 · Buyer activity: the flow score

The flow score (0–100) combines four Cotality signals. Each month, every council area with 100+ sales a year is ranked against all the others on each signal; the four ranks are averaged and ranked again. 70+ buyers arriving (top 30%), 30–69 neutral, below 30 buyers leaving. Across 2005–2025 the top fifth grew 9.8% the next year against 2.8% for the bottom fifth. The four signals are shown with their raw value and their rank (0 = worst, 100 = best) underneath:

  1. Sales volume, 12-month change: rising = buyers coming back.
  2. Listings, 12-month change: falling = supply drying up.
  3. Days on market, 6-month change: falling = selling faster.
  4. Vendor discount, 6-month change: narrowing = sellers gaining bargaining power.

Source: Cotality Market Trends; flow score built by PP (see the Market Flow Forecast tool for the backtest). Ranks are against every Australian council area with 100+ sales in the last 12 months, capital cities placed against that same set. Cotality changed its days-on-market and discount methods in Jul 2018, May 2020 and Nov 2024; 6-month changes that span those breaks are left out of the score.

8 · Pre-run fingerprint: does it look like Darwin and Townsville before they ran?

Townsville's run started in Mar–Apr 2024 (we entered Jul 2023) and Darwin's in Nov 2025 (we entered Aug 2024). "Run start" = the first month 12-month price growth passed 8% and stayed up. In the 6–12 months before those runs, both markets shared six conditions. This section scores every region against them today. Days on market, sales volume and rent growth differed between the two, so they're left out.

  1. Prices flat: 12-month growth within ±7% and 3-year growth in the bottom third of council areas (half credit: 12-month growth up to +10%).
  2. High yield: gross yield in the top 20% of council areas (half: top 40%). Before their runs: 5.9–7.7%, rank 84–96.
  3. Buyer flow already strong: flow score 70+ (half: 55+). Before their runs: 66–96, while prices were still flat.
  4. Listings falling: down more than 5% on a year earlier (half: down at all).
  5. Supply well below normal: FY26 approvals 20%+ below the previous 10-year average (half: 5%+ below). Before their runs: −28% to −45%.
  6. Vacancy around 2% or below: 12-month average ≤2.2% (half: ≤2.6%).

The four striped rows pinned at the top are reference snapshots: Darwin and Townsville 12 and 6 months before their runs, scored the same way. Darwin and Townsville also appear further down as they are today, marked "today". Click a region to see where it sits against them on each condition.

✓ meets it½ partly✗ doesn't

Based on two buying regions (four markets, houses and units), so treat it as a pattern to watch, not a proven rule. Approvals and vacancy cover all dwellings; the other conditions use the selected property type. Melbourne is not used as a reference because it hasn't run yet.

Summary · Where each region is in its cycle

Pulling the sections together, each region is placed in a stage using three things: 12-month price growth (flat ≤ 8%, or rising), the flow score (are buyers arriving: 70+ strong, below 55 weak), and its 6-month change (are buyers increasing or fading). Running is split by 3-year growth: early stage = 3-year growth still in the bottom 40% of council areas, so the run has only just begun. ▲ = buying region. Each chip shows 12-month growth · flow score (6-month change). Click a region to open its flow chart.

Rules, in order. If 12-month growth is above 8%: flow score below 55, or down 20+ points in 6 months → running: late / cooling; otherwise running: early stage (3-year growth in the bottom 40%) or running: mid stage. If prices are flat (≤ 8%): flow 70+ and rising or listings falling, or flow 55+ and rising, or up 20+ points to 45+ → about to run / likely to run; everything else → not running yet (flat with weak or fading buyer flow).
